1	---
2	title: Check constraints
3	description: Learn how to configure CHECK constraints for data validation with Prisma ORM and PostgreSQL
4	url: /orm/v7/more/troubleshooting/check-constraints
5	metaTitle: Data validation with CHECK constraints (PostgreSQL)
6	metaDescription: Learn how to configure CHECK constraints for data validation with Prisma ORM and PostgreSQL by following the step-by-step instructions in this practical guide.
7	---
8	
9	This page explains how to configure [check constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.4/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-CHECK-CONSTRAINTS) in a PostgreSQL database. A check constraint is a condition that must be satisfied before a value can be saved to a table - for example, the discounted price of a product must always be less than the original price.
10	
11	Check constraints can be added when you create the table (using `CREATE TABLE`) or to a table that already exists (using `ALTER TABLE`).
12	
13	## Prerequisites
14	
15	- A [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) database server running
16	- The [`psql`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/13/app-psql.html) command line client
17	- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) installed
18	
19	## Single column check constraint
20	
21	Create a table with a check constraint on a single column:
22	
23	```sql
24	CREATE TABLE "public"."product" (
25	  price NUMERIC CONSTRAINT price_value_check CHECK (price > 0.01 AND price <> 1240.00)
26	);
27	ALTER TABLE "public"."product"
28	  ADD COLUMN "productid" serial,
29	  ADD PRIMARY KEY ("productid");
30	```
31	
32	This ensures the price is never less than 0.01 and never equal to 1240.00.
33	
34	## Multi-column check constraint
35	
36	Create a table with a check constraint that compares values of two columns:
37	
38	```sql
39	CREATE TABLE "public"."anotherproduct" (
40	  reducedprice NUMERIC CONSTRAINT reduced_price_check CHECK (price > reducedprice),
41	  price NUMERIC
42	);
43	ALTER TABLE "public"."anotherproduct"
44	  ADD COLUMN "productid" serial,
45	  ADD PRIMARY KEY ("productid");
46	```
47	
48	This ensures `reducedprice` is always less than `price`.
49	
50	## Multiple check constraints
51	
52	```sql
53	CREATE TABLE "public"."secondtolastproduct" (
54	  reducedprice NUMERIC CONSTRAINT reduced_price_check CHECK (price > reducedprice),
55	  price NUMERIC,
56	  tags TEXT[] CONSTRAINT tags_contains_product CHECK ('product' = ANY(tags))
57	);
58	ALTER TABLE "public"."secondtolastproduct"
59	  ADD COLUMN "productid" serial,
60	  ADD PRIMARY KEY ("productid");
61	```
62	
63	## Adding check constraints to existing tables
64	
65	```sql
66	CREATE TABLE "public"."lastproduct" (
67	  category TEXT
68	);
69	
70	ALTER TABLE "public"."lastproduct"
71	  ADD CONSTRAINT "category_not_clothing" CHECK (category <> 'clothing');
72	```
73	
74	## Using with Prisma ORM
75	
76	After introspection, your Prisma schema will include the models but the check constraints are enforced at the database level:
77	
78	```prisma
79	model product {
80	  price     Float?
81	  productid Int    @id
82	}
83	
84	model anotherproduct {
85	  price        Float?
86	  productid    Int    @id
87	  reducedprice Float?
88	}
89	```
90	
91	Generate Prisma Client and test:
92	
93	```js
94	const { PrismaClient } = require("../prisma/generated/client");
95	
96	const prisma = new PrismaClient();
97	
98	async function main() {
99	  // This will fail due to the check constraint
100	  const newProduct = await prisma.product.create({
101	    data: {
102	      price: 0.0, // violates price > 0.01
103	    },
104	  });
105	}
106	
107	main();
108	```
109	
110	The script throws an error indicating the `price_check_value` check constraint was not met:
111	
112	```
113	Error: new row for relation "product" violates check constraint "price_value_check"
114	```
115	
116	Check constraints are resolved in alphabetical order, and only the first constraint to fail appears in the error message.
117

1	---
2	title: Customizing migrations
3	description: How to edit a migration file before applying it to avoid data loss in production.
4	url: /orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations
5	metaTitle: Customizing migrations
6	metaDescription: How to edit a migration file before applying it to avoid data loss in production.
7	---
8	
9	In some scenarios, you need to edit a migration file before you apply it. For example, to [change the direction of a 1-1 relation](#example-change-the-direction-of-a-1-1-relation) (moving the foreign key from one side to another) without data loss, you need to move data as part of the migration - this SQL is not part of the default migration, and must be written by hand.
10	
11	This guide explains how to edit migration files and gives some examples of use cases where you may want to do this.
12	
13	## How to edit a migration file
14	
15	To edit a migration file before applying it, the general procedure is the following:
16	
17	- Make a schema change that requires custom SQL (for example, to preserve existing data)
18	- Create a draft migration using:
19	
20	```npm
21	npx prisma migrate dev --create-only
22	```
23	
24	- Modify the generated SQL file.
25	- Apply the modified SQL by running:
26	
27	```npm
28	npx prisma migrate dev
29	```
30	
31	### Example: Rename a field
32	
33	By default, renaming a field in the schema results in a migration that will:
34	
35	- `CREATE` a new column (for example, `fullname`)
36	- `DROP` the existing column (for example, `name`) and the data in that column
37	
38	To actually **rename** a field and avoid data loss when you run the migration in production, you need to modify the generated migration SQL before applying it to the database. Consider the following schema fragment - the `biograpy` field is spelled wrong.
39	
40	```prisma highlight=3;normal; title="schema.prisma"
41	model Profile {
42	  id       Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
43	  biograpy String // [!code highlight]
44	  userId   Int    @unique
45	  user     User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
46	}
47	```
48	
49	To rename the `biograpy` field to `biography`:
50	
51	Rename the field in the schema:
52	
53	```prisma highlight=3;delete|4;add; title="schema.prisma
54	model Profile {
55	  id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
56	  biograpy  String // [!code --]
57	  biography String // [!code ++]
58	  userId    Int    @unique
59	  user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
60	}
61	```
62	
63	- Run the following command to create a **draft migration** that you can edit before applying to the database:
64	
65	```npm
66	npx prisma migrate dev --name rename-migration --create-only
67	```
68	
69	- Edit the draft migration as shown, changing `DROP` / `DELETE` to a single `RENAME COLUMN`:
70	
71	```sql title="migration.sql" tab="Before"
72	ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP COLUMN "biograpy",
73	ADD COLUMN  "biography" TEXT NOT NULL;
74	```
75	
76	```sql title="migration.sql" tab="After"
77	ALTER TABLE "Profile"
78	RENAME COLUMN "biograpy" TO "biography"
79	```
80	
81	- Save and apply the migration:
82	
83	```npm
84	npx prisma migrate dev
85	```
86	
87	You can use the same technique to rename a `model` - edit the generated SQL to _rename_ the table rather than drop and re-create it.
88	
89	### Example: Use the expand and contract pattern to evolve the schema without downtime
90	
91	Making schema changes to existing fields, e.g., renaming a field can lead to downtime. It happens in the time frame between applying a migration that modifies an existing field, and deploying a new version of the application code which uses the modified field.
92	
93	You can prevent downtime by breaking down the steps required to alter a field into a series of discrete steps designed to introduce the change gradually. This pattern is known as the _expand and contract pattern_.
94	
95	The pattern involves two components: your application code accessing the database and the database schema you intend to alter.
96	
97	With the _expand and contract_ pattern, renaming the field `bio` to `biography` would look as follows with Prisma:
98	
99	- Add the new `biography` field to your Prisma schema and create a migration
100	
101	```prisma highlight=4;add; title="schema.prisma"
102	model Profile {
103	 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
104	 bio       String
105	 biography String // [!code ++]
106	 userId    Int    @unique
107	 user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
108	}
109	```
110	
111	- _Expand_: update the application code and write to both the `bio` and `biography` fields, but continue reading from the `bio` field, and deploy the code
112	- Create an empty migration and copy existing data from the `bio` to the `biography` field
113	
114	```npm
115	npx prisma migrate dev --name copy_biography --create-only
116	```
117	
118	```sql title="migration.sql"
119	UPDATE "Profile" SET biography = bio;
120	```
121	
122	4. Verify the integrity of the `biography` field in the database
123	5. Update application code to **read** from the new `biography` field
124	6. Update application code to **stop writing** to the `bio` field
125	7. _Contract_: remove the `bio` from the Prisma schema, and create a migration to remove the `bio` field
126	
127	```prisma highlight=3;delete; title="schema.prisma"
128	model Profile {
129	 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
130	 bio       String // [!code --]
131	 biography String
132	 userId    Int    @unique
133	 user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
134	}
135	```
136	
137	```npm
138	npx prisma migrate dev --name remove_bio
139	```
140	
141	By using this approach, you avoid potential downtime that altering existing fields that are used in the application code are prone to, and reduce the amount of coordination required between applying the migration and deploying the updated application code.
142	
143	Note that this pattern is applicable in any situation involving a change to a column that has data and is in use by the application code. Examples include combining two fields into one, or transforming a `1:n` relation to a `m:n` relation.
144	
145	To learn more, check out the Data Guide article on [the expand and contract pattern](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/types/relational/expand-and-contract-pattern)
146	
147	### Example: Change the direction of a 1-1 relation
148	
149	To change the direction of a 1-1 relation:
150	
151	- Make the change in the schema:
152	
153	```prisma title="schema.prisma"
154	model User {
155	 id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
156	 name      String
157	 posts     Post[]
158	 profile   Profile? @relation(fields: [profileId], references: [id])
159	 profileId Int      @unique
160	}
161	
162	model Profile {
163	 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
164	 biography String
165	 user      User
166	}
167	```
168	
169	- Run the following command to create a **draft migration** that you can edit before applying to the database:
170	
171	```npm
172	npx prisma migrate dev --name rename-migration --create-only
173	```
174	
175	```text
176	⚠️  There will be data loss when applying the migration:
177	
178	• The migration will add a unique constraint covering the columns `[profileId]` on the table `User`. If there are existing duplicate values, the migration will fail.
179	```
180	
181	- Edit the draft migration as shown:
182	
183	```sql title="migration" tab="Before"
184	-- DropForeignKey
185	ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP CONSTRAINT "Profile_userId_fkey";
186	
187	-- DropIndex
188	DROP INDEX "Profile_userId_unique";
189	
190	-- AlterTable
191	ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP COLUMN "userId";
192	
193	-- AlterTable
194	ALTER TABLE "User" ADD COLUMN     "profileId" INTEGER NOT NULL;
195	
196	-- CreateIndex
197	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "User_profileId_unique" ON "User"("profileId");
198	
199	-- AddForeignKey
200	ALTER TABLE "User" ADD FOREIGN KEY ("profileId") REFERENCES "Profile"("id") ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE;
201	```
202	
203	```sql title="migration" tab="After"
204	-- DropForeignKey
205	ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP CONSTRAINT "Profile_userId_fkey";
206	
207	-- DropIndex
208	DROP INDEX "Profile_userId_unique";
209	
210	-- AlterTable
211	ALTER TABLE "User" ADD COLUMN "profileId" INTEGER;
212	
213	UPDATE "User"
214	SET "profileId" = "Profile".id
215	FROM "Profile"
216	WHERE "User".id = "Profile"."userId";
217	
218	ALTER TABLE "User" ALTER COLUMN "profileId" SET NOT NULL;
219	
220	-- AlterTable
221	ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP COLUMN "userId";
222	
223	-- CreateIndex
224	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "User_profileId_unique" ON "User"("profileId");
225	
226	-- AddForeignKey
227	ALTER TABLE "User" ADD FOREIGN KEY ("profileId") REFERENCES "Profile"("id") ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE;
228	```
229	
230	- Save and apply the migration:
231	
232	```npm
233	npx prisma migrate dev
234	```
235

---
title: Customizing migrations
description: How to edit a migration file before applying it to avoid data loss in production.
url: /orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations
metaTitle: Customizing migrations
metaDescription: How to edit a migration file before applying it to avoid data loss in production.
---

In some scenarios, you need to edit a migration file before you apply it. For example, to [change the direction of a 1-1 relation](#example-change-the-direction-of-a-1-1-relation) (moving the foreign key from one side to another) without data loss, you need to move data as part of the migration - this SQL is not part of the default migration, and must be written by hand.

This guide explains how to edit migration files and gives some examples of use cases where you may want to do this.

## How to edit a migration file

To edit a migration file before applying it, the general procedure is the following:

- Make a schema change that requires custom SQL (for example, to preserve existing data)
- Create a draft migration using:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --create-only
```

- Modify the generated SQL file.
- Apply the modified SQL by running:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev
```

### Example: Rename a field

By default, renaming a field in the schema results in a migration that will:

- `CREATE` a new column (for example, `fullname`)
- `DROP` the existing column (for example, `name`) and the data in that column

To actually **rename** a field and avoid data loss when you run the migration in production, you need to modify the generated migration SQL before applying it to the database. Consider the following schema fragment - the `biograpy` field is spelled wrong.

```prisma highlight=3;normal; title="schema.prisma"
model Profile {
  id       Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  biograpy String // [!code highlight]
  userId   Int    @unique
  user     User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
}
```

To rename the `biograpy` field to `biography`:

Rename the field in the schema:

```prisma highlight=3;delete|4;add; title="schema.prisma
model Profile {
  id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  biograpy  String // [!code --]
  biography String // [!code ++]
  userId    Int    @unique
  user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
}
```

- Run the following command to create a **draft migration** that you can edit before applying to the database:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name rename-migration --create-only
```

- Edit the draft migration as shown, changing `DROP` / `DELETE` to a single `RENAME COLUMN`:

```sql title="migration.sql" tab="Before"
ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP COLUMN "biograpy",
ADD COLUMN  "biography" TEXT NOT NULL;
```

```sql title="migration.sql" tab="After"
ALTER TABLE "Profile"
RENAME COLUMN "biograpy" TO "biography"
```

- Save and apply the migration:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev
```

You can use the same technique to rename a `model` - edit the generated SQL to _rename_ the table rather than drop and re-create it.

### Example: Use the expand and contract pattern to evolve the schema without downtime

Making schema changes to existing fields, e.g., renaming a field can lead to downtime. It happens in the time frame between applying a migration that modifies an existing field, and deploying a new version of the application code which uses the modified field.

You can prevent downtime by breaking down the steps required to alter a field into a series of discrete steps designed to introduce the change gradually. This pattern is known as the _expand and contract pattern_.

The pattern involves two components: your application code accessing the database and the database schema you intend to alter.

With the _expand and contract_ pattern, renaming the field `bio` to `biography` would look as follows with Prisma:

- Add the new `biography` field to your Prisma schema and create a migration

```prisma highlight=4;add; title="schema.prisma"
model Profile {
 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
 bio       String
 biography String // [!code ++]
 userId    Int    @unique
 user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
}
```

- _Expand_: update the application code and write to both the `bio` and `biography` fields, but continue reading from the `bio` field, and deploy the code
- Create an empty migration and copy existing data from the `bio` to the `biography` field

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name copy_biography --create-only
```

```sql title="migration.sql"
UPDATE "Profile" SET biography = bio;
```

4. Verify the integrity of the `biography` field in the database
5. Update application code to **read** from the new `biography` field
6. Update application code to **stop writing** to the `bio` field
7. _Contract_: remove the `bio` from the Prisma schema, and create a migration to remove the `bio` field

```prisma highlight=3;delete; title="schema.prisma"
model Profile {
 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
 bio       String // [!code --]
 biography String
 userId    Int    @unique
 user      User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
}
```

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name remove_bio
```

By using this approach, you avoid potential downtime that altering existing fields that are used in the application code are prone to, and reduce the amount of coordination required between applying the migration and deploying the updated application code.

Note that this pattern is applicable in any situation involving a change to a column that has data and is in use by the application code. Examples include combining two fields into one, or transforming a `1:n` relation to a `m:n` relation.

To learn more, check out the Data Guide article on [the expand and contract pattern](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/types/relational/expand-and-contract-pattern)

### Example: Change the direction of a 1-1 relation

To change the direction of a 1-1 relation:

- Make the change in the schema:

```prisma title="schema.prisma"
model User {
 id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
 name      String
 posts     Post[]
 profile   Profile? @relation(fields: [profileId], references: [id])
 profileId Int      @unique
}

model Profile {
 id        Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
 biography String
 user      User
}
```

- Run the following command to create a **draft migration** that you can edit before applying to the database:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name rename-migration --create-only
```

```text
⚠️  There will be data loss when applying the migration:

• The migration will add a unique constraint covering the columns `[profileId]` on the table `User`. If there are existing duplicate values, the migration will fail.
```

- Edit the draft migration as shown:

```sql title="migration" tab="Before"
-- DropForeignKey
ALTER TABLE "Profile" DROP CONSTRAINT "Profile_userId_fkey";

-- DropIndex
DROP INDEX "Profile_userId_unique";
```

**Best practice:** run `npx prisma migrate dev --create-only` first, then edit the generated `migration.sql` to append your `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...)` statement before applying with `npx prisma migrate dev`.

- Source: `apps/docs/content/docs/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations.mdx` (§"How to edit a migration file") — the documented pattern is `--create-only` → edit `migration.sql` → apply.
- Since check constraints aren't representable in the Prisma schema (see `apps/docs/content/docs/orm/v7/more/troubleshooting/check-constraints.mdx`), Prisma won't ever try to "fix" or drop your constraint on future auto-generated migrations, so editing the same auto-generated file is fine — no need for a separate empty migration.
